PUBLIC LEGAL NOTICE

Date: 25th July 2026 

TO:
1. THE UNIDENTIFIED INDIVIDUAL (JANE DOE) 
Featured in Subject Instagram Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)

2. THE GRIEVANCE OFFICER & LEGAL CELL
  Meta Platforms, Inc. / Instagram LLC
  (Intermediary hosting subject digital broadcast)

3. TO WHOMSOEVER IT MAY CONCERN / GENERAL PUBLIC
SUBJECT: LEGAL NOTICE DEMANDING CEASE & DESIST, IMMEDIATE TAKEDOWN OF UNLAWFUL DIGITAL CONTENT, PUBLIC RETRACTION, AND INITIATION OF PROCEEDINGS UNDER THE BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA (BNS), 2023 AND THE INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY ACT, 2000.

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:
   a) Section 351 (Criminal Intimidation);
   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

In light of the statutory breaches detailed above, you are hereby called upon to comply with the following requisites within SEVEN (7) DAYS from the date of this Notice:
A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

B. TAKEDOWN AND DELETION - Ensure the immediate deletion and permanent takedown of the impugned Reel (URL: https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY)from Instagram and all mirror platforms.

C. PUBLIC APOLOGY / RETRACTION- Issue an unconditional public apology across official digital channels acknowledging the improper nature of the broadcast and expressing regret.
 
TAKE NOTICE that if you fail to strictly comply with the terms of this Legal Notice within the stipulated period of 7 (Seven) days, it shall be constrained to initiate appropriate civil and criminal proceedings against you—including filing a formal First Information Report (FIR) under the relevant provisions of BNS, 2023 read with Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000, alongside seeking direction from the competent Judicial Magistrate under Section 175(3) of BNSS, 2023—entirely at your risk, cost, and legal consequences.
 
A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

Shruti Dixit
Advocate
Rajasthan High Court

text:
Open Letter to @Meta , @finkd , @mosseri @instagram @kunalb11  @facebook @WhatsApp , and Everyone Watching

@Meta ,

You built platforms that hold our memories, our businesses, our friendships, our work. Then you handed the keys to AI and walked away.

Accounts on Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp are being disabled or suspended overnight by automated systems. No clear reason. No warning. No human in the loop. Just a bot decision that can erase years of life in seconds.

Sometimes you send an email later saying “we made a mistake, you can use the account again.” Then nothing changes. The account stays locked. Or worse while it’s locked in appeal, it gets compromised. Unauthorized recovery numbers appear. Hidden apps show up. Codes stop working. And the person who built that account for a decade is left staring at recovery screens that keep changing.

When accounts finally come back, if they come back at all, it’s often just a quiet “sorry.” No explanation. No accountability. 

No acknowledgment of what the user went through while they were locked out  the panic, the lost clients, the family photos they couldn’t reach, the nights spent arguing with a chatbot that loops forever.

This is not a rare glitch anymore. It’s a pattern. AI is deciding who gets to keep their digital life, and when it gets it wrong, there is almost no path to a real human.

Meta Verified users, people who filed cybercrime complaints, people who used the official Grievance Officer process under the IT Rules many of them are still waiting. The support system points them back to the same AI that caused the problem.

We are not asking you to stop using AI. We are asking you to stop letting it act alone on decisions that destroy livelihoods and memories. When the system fails, a human must be able to step in. When you admit an error, you must actually fix it. When someone is locked out for weeks, “sorry” is not enough.

To everyone who has lost an account, waited for a human that never came, or watched their years of work disappear into an appeal that never ends: you are not alone, and you are not imagining this. The trauma is real. The silence is not acceptable.

Meta, the platforms you run are not just products. They hold pieces of people’s lives. Treat them that way.

We demand human review for account-level actions. Clear reasons. Working appeals. Real accountability when AI gets it wrong.

#MetaHumanReview #JusticeForInstagramUsers #ProtestAgainstMeta  
@Meta @instagram @facebook @WhatsApp @mosseri @finkd

If this happened to you, share your story. If it hasn’t yet, it can. Amplify this until they cannot ignore the cost of their automation.

Regards 
A Disappointed Meta User

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

text:
The Delhi High Court has issued notice on a constitutional challenge to the automated filter which Meta operates on Instagram and Facebook in India, and to Rule 4(4) of the IT Rules, 2021. On 19 November 2026, the Court issued notice to the Union of India and to Meta on a writ petition filed by Live Law Media Private Limited and its Director, Sindhu T.P. IFF is supporting LiveLaw in this challenge. (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/s5ichxKjPu

In October 2026, MeitY also issued two advisories which it has not published. The second, dated 10 October and addressed to Meta alone, asks for “enhanced diligence” and for action “with immediate effect”. Neither the IT Act nor the IT Rules gives MeitY the power to issue such advisories. A restriction on speech must rest on a law, and a departmental instruction is not one. (8/10)

The petition contends that Rule 4(4) exceeds the powers conferred by the IT Act, creates a blocking regime outside Section 69A, and operates as a prior restraint on the press. A publisher whose report is suppressed by automated tools receives no notice, no reasons and no hearing. The grievance route offers little, since 54,918 appeals were pending before the Grievance Appellate Committee on 2 November 2026. (9/10)

CENTRE TELLS SC AHMEDABAD CRASH PROBE NEARLY DONE

The Centre told the Supreme Court on Wednesday that its probe into the June 12, 2025 Air India crash in Ahmedabad has entered its closing stage. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta sought a two to three week adjournment, saying investigators must finish work under international procedures.

The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau had earlier been expected to place its draft final report before the court in early October, in a sealed cover. Petitioners, including the father of the deceased pilot and the Safety Matters Foundation, want an independent, court supervised probe and public release of the final report.

The AAIB said cockpit voice and airborne image recordings cannot be shared with an outside committee or the public under the Aircraft (Investigation of Accidents and Incidents) Rules, 2025. Flight AI-171, a Boeing 787-8 headed to London Gatwick, crashed soon after leaving Ahmedabad. It killed 260 people, including former Gujarat chief minister Vijay Rupani.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) has mandated a new four-layer structure for all private car and two-wheeler insurance policies issued or renewed from December 15, replacing the existing standalone act-only and comprehensive formats with a single unified form.

The framework splits coverage into four standardized parts:
1. Third-party liability (Compulsory)
2. Personal accident cover for the owner-driver (Compulsory; optional for other occupants)
3. Legal liability towards passengers/occupants (Optional)
4. Own-damage cover (Optional)

The change follows a Supreme Court ruling on August 4 in National Insurance Vs Thungala Dhana Laxmi. Under the new system, policyholders must explicitly opt in or opt out of non-mandatory sections. While third-party rates remain regulated, insurers will independently price the other three components.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

New Delhi, 1 July 2026

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Can the Government suspend a political party’s Instagram handle without a clear statutory power? And can a politician boycott a courtroom while simultaneously asking the Supreme Court to transfer the same judge from hearing his case?  

This week, the Aam Aadmi Party raised both questions in two different constitutional courtrooms.  

In the Supreme Court, AAP challenged the suspension of its Gujarat unit’s Instagram handle, arguing that Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act was never meant to become a direct content-blocking weapon. 

Senior Advocate Shadan Farasat argued that the provision only deals with “safe harbour” obligations of intermediaries — not independent censorship powers.  The party says the move violates Article 19(1)(a), the constitutional guarantee of free speech. 

The Supreme Court has now issued notice to the Centre.  At the same time in the Delhi High Court, Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma appointed three amicus curiae for Arvind Kejriwal, Manish Sisodia, and Satyendar Jain after the leaders chose to boycott proceedings, invoking “Mahatma Gandhi’s Satyagraha principles” and claiming their faith in the court process had been shaken.  

But here’s the constitutional twist: Kejriwal had also moved the Supreme Court seeking transfer of the excise policy case away from Justice Sharma’s bench — even as his legal team withdrew from participation before her court.  

This has now created a rare constitutional confrontation involving: 
⚖️ Article 19 vs state regulation of digital speech 
⚖️ Article 21 vs procedural fairness in criminal prosecution 
⚖️ Judicial recusal vs courtroom boycott 
⚖️ Free speech, due process, and strategic constitutional litigation  Justice Sharma’s response may become one of the most significant procedural moments in the case: instead of proceeding ex parte, she chose to appoint independent senior advocates as amicus curiae to preserve procedural fairness.  

And one line from the Supreme Court hearing may define this entire battle: “Today my portal is gone.”  Because this is no longer just about an Instagram account.

 It is about whether opposition parties in India can lose their digital voice overnight — and what constitutional remedy exists when that happens.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

A $260M exit taught me: order less inventory than you want.

I ran operations and finance while we bootstrapped Hiya Health to nine figures in US sales annually. Growth eats cash before it produces cash, and inventory is usually where it goes.

How I'd size your next order:

1. Order less than your forecast says. A stockout costs you a few sales. Dead inventory costs you the cash you needed for everything else.

2. Price the second risk of over-ordering: you may not have product-market fit yet. If customers tell you to change the formula, the flavor, the packaging... what happens to a warehouse full of the old version?

3. Pay for shorter lead times over cheaper unit costs. A supplier who costs 10% more but ships in half the time lets you order smaller and reorder faster.

4. Air-ship early runs even though it stings. Until you know what sells, speed to learning matters more than cost per unit.

5. Map every delay to a dollar. Every week of lead time either ties up cash or costs you a sale.

The mistake I see founders make is in the sequencing... they lock in too much inventory to save on unit cost, then can't afford the marketing to sell it.

If you want me to pressure-test your next order before you wire the deposit, DM me. It's the kind of thing I dig into with founders in The Builder's Room every month.

𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐚𝐧 𝐎𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐥𝐞: 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐬

You built a billing agent that nailed its demo. Six weeks in production it refunds $940 on a $120 account because nobody checked the amount against invoices before hitting the payment API. The demo never needed that check - the customer's quoted amount matched what was actually billed.

The obvious move is upgrading the model. The tempting justification is LangChain's +13.7 on Terminal Bench 2.0 with the model held still. But here's the problem: that result was scored by tests your agent does not have. The oracle that validated LangChain's coding harness - running unit tests in a sandbox - does not exist in your domain.

What transfers and what doesn't comes down to where the oracle sits in the harness lifecycle.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬:

A measurement oracle scores runs after the fact - that's how published numbers get published. A selection oracle guides improvements while you're building the harness. An in-loop oracle runs during execution, giving the agent a verdict before it stops. LangChain's verify-before-exit step needed an in-loop oracle - deterministic code that fires mid-run. The hook transfers when you move it in front of each action. What doesn't transfer: the oracle running tests behind it. In a refund queue with no external feedback loop wired in, that verification step runs after money moves, making self-correction your only lever. The mechanism that carries over is the interception point, not the reminder.

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐚 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤:

A model upgrade handles demo inputs better and shifts ordinary production failures into rare, costly edge cases. It doesn't close the demo cliff - it moves where the cliff sits. The inputs your prompt author never showed the agent still fail. Without a harness that catches them, a newer model just fails at higher confidence.

The core insight: borrowed evidence from coding agents only holds if your domain has the same oracle structure. Ceilings and thresholds transfer as mechanisms. Self-verification without external checks does not. Build your harness around what your production environment can actually measure.

🔸The Challenge to the DPDP Act
- Petitioner
DNPA (21 publishers); petition filed 6 October, stay sought 27 October.

- Concerns
Could expose sources, force removal of reports and deter whistleblowers.

- Consent problem
Seeking consent from subjects = 'pre-censorship' (Madhavi Divan).

- No exemption
The Act has no specific journalistic exemption.

🔸Relevant Provisions of the DPDP Act
- Section 3(c)(ii)
Excludes data made public by the person or under a legal duty – a limited exclusion.

- Sections 4–6
Grounds, notice and consent for processing personal data.

- Section 8
Duties of data fiduciaries – security, accuracy, erasure.

- Section 17
Exemptions for legal proceedings, law enforcement, research – not journalism.

🔸The Constitutional Balance
- Right to Privacy
Article 21 – dignity, autonomy, personal data (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017).

- Press freedom
Article 19(1)(a) – investigate and report on public interest.

- Limits
Both are not absolute; Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions.

🔸Key Judgments
- R. Rajagopal (1994)
'Auto Shankar case' – officials can't use privacy to block reports on official conduct; no prior restraint.

- R.K. Anand (2009)
Upheld a sting operation exposing an attempt to subvert the BMW trial.

- Manu Sharma (2010)
Warned against media trials that turn suspects into convicts.

- Sahara v. SEBI (2012)
Courts may postpone reporting if there is real risk to a fair trial.

- Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014)
Sting journalism gives no blanket immunity for unlawful acts.

- Axel Springer v. Germany (2012)
ECHR Grand Chamber (12–5) upheld a newspaper's report on an actor's arrest as public-interest journalism.

🔸Global Approaches
- USA
First Amendment; Privacy Protection Act, 1980 limits searches of journalists' work.

- UK
Data Protection Act, 2018 – exemption if publication is in the public interest.

- Brazil
General Data Protection Law excludes journalisticprocessing.

- Kenya
Section 52, Data Protection Act, 2019 – conditional exemption.

- International law
Articles 17 & 19 ICCPR; Articles 8 & 10 ECHR.

🔸Way Forward
- Journalistic exemption
A narrow, public-interest exemption in the DPDP framework.

- Public interest test
Separate genuine scrutiny from needless intrusion.

- Source protection
Protect sources while ensuring accuracy and fairness.

- Proportionality
Restrictions must be necessary and proportionate.

Privacy vs Press Freedom: Where Should the Line Be Drawn?

Introduction

🌟 The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, has reignited the constitutional debate between individual privacy and freedom of the press. The challenge is to protect personal dignity without undermining investigative journalism and the public's right to know.

Main Body

🌟 Constitutional Balance: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of expression, while Article 21 protects the right to privacy, recognised in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

🌟 Journalistic Independence: Mandatory consent for personal information could restrict investigative reporting and discourage whistleblowers from exposing wrongdoing.

🌟 Public Interest Test: In R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (1994), the Supreme Court distinguished legitimate public reporting from unjustified intrusion into private life.

🌟 Sting Operations: R.K. Anand v. Registrar, Delhi High Court (2009) recognised their public value in exposing misconduct, while Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014) cautioned against treating sting operations as immunity from criminal liability.

🌟 Media Accountability: Sahara v. SEBI (2012) recognised temporary postponement of publication where publicity threatens a fair trial.

🌟 International Practice: The US, UK, Brazil and Kenya provide different forms of journalistic exemptions within data-protection frameworks.

Challenges

🌟 Balancing privacy with transparency and accountability.

🌟 Protecting confidential sources and whistleblowers.

🌟 Preventing trial by media and reputational damage.

🌟 Avoiding misuse of privacy laws to suppress scrutiny.

Constructive Criticism

🌟 Excessive consent requirements may create indirect censorship.

🌟 Unclear exemptions can generate regulatory uncertainty.

🌟 Investigative journalism may become vulnerable to legal intimidation.

🌟 Unrestricted reporting can violate individual dignity and fair-trial rights.

Way Forward

🌟 Introduce a clearly defined public-interest exemption.

🌟 Establish independent and proportionate oversight.

🌟 Protect confidential journalistic sources.

🌟 Develop safeguards against trial by media.

🌟 Harmonise data protection with constitutional freedoms.

Highlighted Keywords

🌟 Constitutional Balancing: Reconciling competing fundamental rights without allowing either to become absolute.

🌟 Public Interest: Information necessary for democratic accountability, not merely public curiosity.

🌟 Prior Restraint: Government-imposed restriction on publication before it occurs.

🌟 Trial by Media: Media coverage that prejudges guilt before judicial determination.

🌟 Proportionality: Restricting a right only to the extent necessary for a legitimate objective.

Conclusion

🌟 A mature democracy must protect both the individual's right to dignity and the press's duty to question power. Privacy must not become a shield for misconduct, nor press freedom a licence for intrusion.

Text of My Keynote Address
Delivered at the National Press Day, 2026 celebrations organised by the National Union of Journalists (India), Hyderabad, on 16 November 2026.

*****

Distinguished office-bearers of the National Union of Journalists (India), members of the journalist fraternity, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen.

My greetings to all of you on #NationalPressDay2026.

I am delighted to address an issue that goes beyond the interests of journalists and media organisations. It concerns the survival of truth, the accountability of power and the foundations of democracy.

Artificial Intelligence is transforming how information is created and disseminated—and how people perceive reality. It offers extraordinary possibilities but also unprecedented dangers. In an age when reality itself can be manufactured, who will defend the truth?

For journalism, this is not merely a technological challenge. It is a test of credibility, independence and courage.

I would like to examine this challenge from a democratic and constitutional perspective.

1. AI AND THE MANUFACTURE OF REALITY

Every major technological revolution has transformed communication. The printing press expanded the dissemination of knowledge; radio and television transformed mass communication; the internet removed geographical barriers. Artificial Intelligence takes this transformation to an entirely different level.

Today, videos, voices, photographs, documents and entire narratives can be fabricated and presented as authentic. The consequences can be devastating: elections manipulated, reputations destroyed, social unrest provoked, national security threatened and the administration of justice compromised.

Yet AI can also assist journalism by analysing vast volumes of information, identifying patterns, translating Indian languages and helping uncover facts.
But one distinction is fundamental: the ability to manufacture information is not the ability to establish truth.

A convincing video is not necessarily genuine evidence. An algorithmically identified pattern is not proof of wrongdoing. A machine can generate a narrative, but it cannot assume responsibility for its veracity.

Verification, corroboration and independent human judgment remain indispensable.

AI may transform the tools of journalism. It must never be allowed to manufacture the truth that journalism is duty-bound to discover.

2. THE PRESS AND DEMOCRACY

A functioning democracy rests on four great institutions: the Legislature, the Executive, the Judiciary and the Free Press. The first three are constitutional organs of the State. The Press has evolved as the Fourth Estate, performing an equally indispensable democratic function.

Our National Emblem offers an interesting metaphor. The Lion Capital of Ashoka depicts four lions standing back to back. Three are visible; the fourth remains invisible. One could metaphorically associate that invisible fourth lion with the Press—not as a constitutional interpretation, but as a reminder of its indispensable democratic role.

The Legislature makes laws, the Executive implements them and the Judiciary interprets them and safeguards the rule of law. The Press informs citizens, scrutinises power, exposes wrongdoing and gives voice to public concerns.

It is the bridge between governance and the people, telling citizens what is done in their name, with their mandate and, most importantly, with their money.

Article 19(1)(a) of our Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression. The Supreme Court has recognised freedom of the Press as integral to this right, subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

Press freedom is not merely a professional privilege. It is also the citizen's right to receive information and form independent opinions.

The Press is not merely an observer of democracy. It enables citizens to question power and hold those who govern them accountable.

3. MEDIA INDEPENDENCE: FROM WHOM AND WHAT?

We frequently discuss press freedom in terms of censorship, governmental interference and intimidation. But the question of independence goes much deeper.

Independence from whom? Independence from what?

Is the Press independent of governments, political parties, corporate owners, commercial interests, ideological and religious influences? Is it independent of its own prejudices?

A Press free from governmental censorship but controlled by political patrons, corporate owners or ideological loyalties is not truly independent.

First: Independence from political ownership and control.

Political parties, politicians and their associates own, control or influence media organisations. At the same time, business interests increasingly enter politics, while politicians acquire commercial interests.
When business becomes politics and politics becomes business, the media becomes an instrument through which both protect their power and interests.

The expression Godi Media has become a widely used pejorative description of sections of the Indian mainstream media since 2014. It reflects the criticism that sections of the media have been manipulated, subdued or co-opted into functioning as publicity and propaganda instruments for the RSS-BJP political establishment and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The problem is not merely favourable coverage. It is the abandonment of scrutiny: governments are praised, opponents vilified and inconvenient questions suppressed.

As the saying goes, “A dog with a bone in its mouth cannot bark.”

Second: Independence from corporate and commercial interests.

Concentration of media ownership, dependence on advertising and commercial pressures can determine editorial priorities. The same business interests may have stakes in media, access to public finance and influence over political decisions.

Between FY2015 and FY2024, scheduled commercial banks wrote off approximately ₹16.35 lakh crore in bad loans, of which around ₹10 lakh crore was linked to big business houses.

Yet, where is the sustained media scrutiny? Where are the investigations into the beneficiaries and the accountability of those responsible?

When the powerful can influence both the flow of public money and the flow of public information, accountability itself is compromised.

Third: Independence of Journalists from Financial Vulnerability.

Journalists must receive fair and assured remuneration and reasonable employment security. Inadequate wages and precarious employment expose them to inducements and pressures that compromise their professional independence. Fair remuneration and employment security are therefore essential safeguards of independent journalism.

Fair remuneration is not merely an employment obligation; it is an essential safeguard of independent journalism.

Fourth: Independence from ideological and religious influence.

Journalists are entitled to personal political, ideological and religious convictions. But personal beliefs must never become professional prejudices. Ideology must not determine which facts are reported, which victims deserve sympathy or which perpetrators are spared scrutiny.

A journalist who applies different standards according to political allegiance or religious identity is practising partisanship, not independent journalism.

The most dangerous form of media control is not always censorship of what is published. It is control over what is never allowed to become a subject of public scrutiny.

Press independence must therefore be both institutional and intellectual: freedom from external control and freedom from prejudices that compromise professional judgment.

4. SELECTIVE JOURNALISM

Media capture by political, corporate and ideological interests has a direct consequence: selective journalism. Some events are amplified, others buried; some victims command national outrage, while others disappear from public consciousness.
Let me cite five examples.

First: Naxalism and Maoist insurgency.

For decades, sections of the intellectual and media establishment romanticised Naxalite and Maoist insurgents as revolutionaries and champions of the oppressed.

Marginalised populations have suffered genuine injustice, exploitation and deprivation. Their grievances deserve redressal. But reporting those grievances is fundamentally different from romanticising armed groups that exploit them to advance a violent, anti-democratic ideology.

Did the media adequately expose how deprivation and alienation were exploited to recruit cadres and perpetuate violence?

When journalism romanticises violent ideologies and neglects their victims, it risks becoming a propaganda instrument and force-multiplier for the very forces it ought to expose.

Second: The genocide and religious cleansing of Kashmiri Hindus.

The genocide and religious cleansing of Kashmiri Hindus from their ancestral homeland remain one of the darkest and most shameful chapters in democratic India's history. Hindus were subjected to targeted killings, terror, threats and religious persecution. An entire Hindu community was driven out of Kashmir, and the Indian State was complicit.

And what did the Indian media do? Where was its outrage? Where were its investigations and sustained campaigns for justice and the safe return of the displaced?

The media's failure was not simply inadequate coverage. It was a complicit silence in the face of the genocide and religious cleansing of an entire community.

By its silence, the media helped erase the suffering of Kashmiri Hindus from the national conscience. That is an indictment of the media as much as it is of the State.

Third: The religious persecution of Hindus in the Northeast.

In the Christian-majority states of Mizoram and Meghalaya, Hindus have been facing severe religious persecution and discrimination. In some instances, they have been denied even the basic right to perform the last rites of their dead, to cremate their own family members in accordance with their religious traditions.

What could be more fundamental than this right? And where is the national media? Where are the headlines, investigations and expressions of outrage?

When the media turns a blind eye to the persecution of a community, it abandons the victims and shields the perpetrators from scrutiny.

Fourth: Double standards in reporting religiously sensitive crimes.

There is a glaring asymmetry in crime reporting. When the victim is Christian or Muslim, or the accused is Hindu, religious identity is often prominently highlighted. But when Hindus are victims, or the accused is Christian or Muslim, that identity disappears into generic descriptions or silence.

Why should the same journalistic standards not apply to everyone?

I demand equal seriousness of investigation, prominence of coverage and accountability, irrespective of the community involved.

The test of secular journalism is not whether it ignores religion, but whether it applies the same standards of fairness and scrutiny to everyone.

Fifth: Neutrality Must Not Become Complicity.

The media cannot be neutral between the perpetrator and the victim. Silence in the face of oppression emboldens the perpetrator and abandons the victim. Neutrality that fails to distinguish between the two is not impartiality; it is complicity.

Journalistic independence demands an unwavering commitment to truth and equal scrutiny of every government, political party, ideology and institution, irrespective of whose interests are affected.

5. FREEDOM AFTER SPEECH

A remark attributed to Idi Amin, the former President of Uganda, captures a fundamental danger: “There is freedom of speech, but I cannot guarantee freedom after speech.”

It exposes the hollowness of a freedom that exists only so long as it does not inconvenience those in power.

This brings me to an important constitutional proposition.

Article 19(1)(a), while guaranteeing freedom of speech and expression, is not adequate by itself to provide the explicit institutional recognition and safeguards that an independent Press requires. The Constitution must recognise the Free Press as an independent Fourth Estate of our democracy.

As National President of the Sarvjan Sanatan Party @sarvjansp, I affirm our commitment to pursuing a constitutional amendment to provide explicit constitutional recognition and status to the Press, so that not only freedom of speech but, importantly, freedom after speech is constitutionally guaranteed and enforced.

If the Press is indispensable to democracy, why should its institutional independence and constitutional status remain without explicit constitutional recognition?

I leave this question before this distinguished gathering.

Thank you.

Statement : Meta told the Home Ministry it acted against 61,000 posts in the fortnight after Chalo Sansad. IFF calls for the record to be made public.

New Delhi, 13 November 2026

Meta has told the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the cybercrime arm of the Ministry of Home Affairs, that it acted on more than 61,000 Facebook and Instagram posts it classified as violent and inciteful between 25 July and 7 August 2026, @ThePrintIndia reported on 12 November. That is about three posts a minute for 14 days. The period begins on the day the Education Minister resigned and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) ended its protest at Jantar Mantar, five days after police used tear gas and a lathi charge against its Chalo Sansad march.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the absence of any public account of this action. Meta disclosed the figure to the Home Ministry at a meeting on 21 August, and it became public only because the minutes were filed in the Supreme Court's suo motu proceedings on digital arrest scams.. In IFF's assessment, the minutes record direct pressure from the Ministry of Home Affairs on the content Meta carries.

As per the report in The Print a meeting was chaired by Rajesh Kumar, I4C's chief executive, and followed reviews by the Union Home Secretary, a parliamentary committee and a court-monitored committee on digital arrests. Its scope was wider than financial fraud. 

According to ThePrint, I4C sought an in-person briefing on "how the algorithm amplifies or suppresses specific content and viral accounts", an analysis of bot networks across prominent handles, and Meta's draft guidelines on deepfakes and re-uploaded content for review.
The minutes, as reported, do not state what the 61,000 posts concerned. It is not known which agency, if any, flagged them, or which law or company rule Meta applied. I4C itself did not accept aggregate figures when Meta cited 70 lakh pieces of content removed, it asked for examples with links. Users and the public are entitled to the same detail.

Complaints received by IFF show what was being restricted on Instagram as the period began. Here we are relying on our own inbound queries and requests for pro-bono help and legal assistance.

1) On 23 July, a story about the protests shared by a private account with 137 followers was made unavailable in India through what Instagram described as "an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements" under the IT Rules, 2021.

2) On 24 July, a reel by the journalist Ila Kazmi showing a Delhi Police facial recognition van scanning protesters at Jantar Mantar was withheld on a notice from "The Government of India / Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", which referred her to the Government of India for any questions. The Delhi High Court has directed the Home Ministry, the IT Ministry, the Delhi Police and Meta to produce the notice and will next hear the case on 17 November.

3) On 28 July, three days after the minister's resignation, Instagram withheld a video published on 15 June by the current-affairs page Unmutezone under the title "Why Modi Can't Ask Dharmendra Pradhan to Resign?". Its editor reported that a second video was blocked on 3 August.

Press reports describe similar restrictions. Newslaundry reported that an interview by the journalist Yaqut Ali with a former CJP spokesperson, posted on 26 July, was blocked in India within minutes, and that Facebook reels on the protests by the creator Jyoti Yadav, including an interview with AAP's Sanjay Singh, were restricted. It later reported restrictions on Instagram posts by Scroll and The Hindu about pellet-gun victims in Kashmir. None of this content is violent or inciteful, and Meta has not said whether it forms part of the figure.

The Home Ministry is involved at each stage from notices under Section 79(3)(b) reach platforms through the Sahyog portal, which I4C operates where close to 1.95 lakh blocking orders were issued to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026, most of them through the portal, and Meta has integrated its systems with it so that flagged content can be restricted without human review. On 27 July the Delhi Police, which reports to the Home Ministry, was reported to have directed platforms to remove posts it considered offensive to the Prime Minister. Meta's transparency report lists violence and incitement among the categories that I4C refers to it. A ministry that operates this channel and also reviews Meta's enforcement figures and algorithm is supervising online speech.

We regret to state that the Supreme Court's own proceedings have provided an avenue for such censorship without sufficient checks and balances. In the suo motu digital arrest case, in which it directed intermediaries to place their proposals before I4C, and in the Just Rights for Children Alliance matters, in which it indicated that platforms may lose safe harbour, the Court has largely acted as a facilitator of executive action rather than as an adjudicator of its constitutional limits. The objectives of curbing fraud and protecting children are legitimate, but the supervision they have enabled now extends to lawful speech and results in censorship without legal authority.

These restrictions do not have a basis in law and often executive rulemaking is being used to circumvent the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. Section 79(3)(b) sets a condition for a platform's immunity and in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court confined it to court orders and government notifications within Article 19(2). The power to block lies in Section 69A, which requires written reasons, committee review and, following Tanul Thakur (2022), a copy of the order and a hearing for the author. Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules requires each intimation to state reasons, the provision, the unlawful act and the URL, and to be reviewed monthly by a Secretary-rank officer. These requirements cannot be met through an automated integration with a three-hour deadline, whatever share of the 61,000 posts came through Sahyog.

Further, we state that while it may constitute a category of harmful speech, "Violent and inciteful" is not a ground for state mandated censorship under Article 19(2). Shreya Singhal protects discussion and advocacy and permits restriction only at the stage of incitement; a video asking why a minister has not resigned is discussion. Nor is there any clear statutory basis for I4C to perform the function of review a platform's content guidelines or to ask which accounts its algorithm promotes.

Our demands

1) The Ministry of Home Affairs must publish the minutes of its meetings with Meta in 2026 and state how many of the 61,000 posts were flagged by I4C, the Delhi Police or any other agency through Sahyog.

2) Meta must publish a breakdown of the 61,000 posts by the rule or law applied, the action taken and the requesting authority, and give each affected user the notice on which it acted. Further monthly breakdowns with qualitative disclosure is necesary.

3) I4C must withdraw its requests to review Meta's draft guidelines and to be briefed on its algorithm. Oversight of this kind requires a law made by Parliament and may only be performed by an independent regulatory body with a clear mandate and objective.

4) The Union Government must publish the monthly Secretary-level reviews under Rule 3(1)(d) for July and August 2026.

5) Meta must end the automatic execution of government and police flags in India and provide human review, a reasoned notice and an opportunity to respond before any restriction.

Users whose posts or accounts were restricted in India in July or August 2026 may write to legal@internetfreedom.in with screenshots of each notice.
